newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian dlr holds gains, lacks local drive.
newsitem.headline: Australian dlr holds gains, lacks local drive.

text.p: The Australian dollar spent Tuesday holding on to its overnight gains that took it back above US$0.8000, but did little else in a consolidative local trading session, dealers said.
After the dollar gained over half of one cent overnight, reaching a high just under US$0.8050, a lack of leads saw it hold to a fairly narrow range in Asian trading.
By 4.45 p.m. the Australian dollar was settled at US$0.8020/25, down slightly on its opening US$0.8026/31, but still up on its local close on Monday of US$0.7983/88.
Key initial resistance and support was at US$0.8050 and US$0.8010 respectively, with traders and analysts seeing a near-term upside test as more likely than a test of support.
"The upward pressure remains intact," BNP Australia technical analyst Clifford Bennett said.
However, any move would be at a more steady pace than the sharp jump that took the unit to US$0.8212 last week, a six year high, analysts said.
In trade weighted terms the unit ended at 59.6, slightly down on the opening 59.7 but up on Monday's closing 59.2.
Against the yen, the Australian dollar closed at 91.08/18 from an early 91.02/12 and a Monday close of 90.19/29, bouyed by a U.S. dollar which firmed above 113.50 yen in Asian trading.
The yen cross survived some morning wobbles after rumours circulated that Bank of Japan Governor Yasuo Matsushita had said long term interest rates bottomed in Japan.
Japanese bond yields also rose in response, but then eased when it became apparent the Matsushita had merely noted that rates had hit another record low.

Speaking before a parliamentary committee this afternoon, Matsushita said the BOJ's monetary policy was geared towards ensuring a firm basis for economic recovery, and he believed that the effects of easier monetary policy may be filtering through the Japanese economy.
Traders said the impetus for moves in the dollar was coming from offshore, despite a range of local data releases this week.

Treasurer Peter Costello is also scheduled to speak in Sydney at an Australian Business Economists dinner later on Tuesday, but the major local event of the week is seen as Thursday's November employment data.
Employment has been one of the weakest areas of the economy in 1996, and a key factor behind the two rate cuts the Reserve Bank has delivered in the second half of this year.
Economists expect employment to have remained weak in November, forecasting it to rise only 10,000 in the month, with the unemployment rate remaining high at 8.7 percent.

On Wednesday, September quarter foreign debt will be released, and although a rise to over A$190 billion from the end June level of A$187.8 billion is expected, market reaction is expected to be muted.

The release of September quarter balance of payments data on Tuesday showing the current account deficit had been financed largely by debt rather than equity confirmed expectations that the debt burden would have risen in the quarter, economists said.
Housing finance data for October is also due on Wednesday.

Although housing is showing some signs of recovery, and anecdotal evidence suggests lending has picked up since the November 6 rate cut, Australian Bankers Association numbers suggest a reasonable sized fall in October lending, economists said.
